statement: English has two tense systems: a primary one marked by verb inflection (preterite vs present) and a secondary one marked by the presence or absence of auxiliary have (perfect vs non-perfect); the two combine into compound tenses.
condition: Applies when describing the tense of a verb phrase: primary tense is preterite or present (inflectional); secondary tense is perfect (have + past participle) or non-perfect; preterite perfect and present perfect are compound tenses.

correct.text: She is believed to have been ill. [perfect, secondary tense]

concept: tense vs time; no future tense
statement: Tense is a grammatical category and time a semantic one: a preterite form need not refer to past time, and since will and shall are modal auxiliaries, English has no future tense.
condition: Applies when assigning tense: the tense category is determined by verb form (preterite vs present), not by the time referred to; will and shall are classed with must, may and can as modal auxiliaries and do not mark a tense.

statement: Grammatical aspect is marked by the presence or absence of auxiliary be (progressive vs non-progressive); the meaning contrast of aspectuality is perfective vs imperfective, and the progressive mainly expresses a kind of imperfective.
condition: Applies when describing progressive verb phrases: aspect (form) is progressive (be + gerund-participle) vs non-progressive; aspectuality (meaning) is perfective (situation viewed as a whole) vs imperfective (viewed from within).

statement: Modal meaning is of three main kinds: deontic (obligation, permission, prohibition), epistemic (speaker's commitment to the truth of the proposition) and dynamic (properties and dispositions, esp. of the subject); all can also be expressed by lexical verbs, adjectives, adverbs and nouns.
condition: Applies when interpreting modal expressions: deontic modality concerns obligation or permission, epistemic modality qualifies the speaker's commitment to truth, dynamic modality concerns the subject's properties or dispositions; non-auxiliary means of expression include lexical verbs, adjectives, adverbs and nouns.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: The same modal can carry different kinds of meaning in different sentences; the book flags 'central cases'. Do not use this as an error-detection rule.

statement: An NP has a determiner and a head nominal; the hierarchy NP > nominal > noun parallels clause > VP > verb; modifiers and complements inside the nominal are internal dependents, while peripheral modifiers and predeterminers are external.
condition: Applies to NP analysis: first split is determiner plus nominal; the nominal contains the head noun and its modifiers or complements (internal dependents); elements like 'quite' and 'all' attach to a whole NP (external dependents); the nominal level may be omitted when there is no modifier or complement.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

statement: An attributive modifier is an internal pre-head dependent in a nominal; it is most often an adjective, but can also be a nominal, a determinative or a verb or VP in gerund-participle or past participle form.
condition: Applies to modifiers before the head noun: adjectival (young), nominal (federal government inquiry), determinative (her many virtues) or verbal (a sleeping child; a frequently overlooked problem).

correct.text: a recently repaired road [VP, past participle]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

statement: With very restricted exceptions, an attributive modifier before the head noun cannot itself contain a post-head dependent.
condition: Applies to a pre-head attributive modifier in a nominal: it may be a simple adjective, nominal or verb form, but may not take its own dependents after it (such as a than-phrase or an adverb following the verb).
violation: A pre-head attributive modifier is followed by its own post-head dependent (e.g. a than-phrase or a post-verbal adverb) before the head noun.

exceptions.description: The source says there are 'very restricted exceptions' but does not list them on this page; the statement 'with only very restricted exceptions' is recorded as is.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Exceptions unlisted here: check Ch. 5 / Ch. 6 before flagging examples with rare modifier patterns as errors.

statement: Direct complements are licensed by the head of the nominal (his fear of the dark; the claim that it was a hoax); indirect complements are licensed by a dependent of the head (a better result than we'd expected; enough time to complete the work) and occur in most kinds of phrase.
condition: Applies to complements in NPs: direct if licensed by the head noun; indirect if licensed by a dependent such as a comparative form or 'enough'.

correct.text: the claim that it was false [direct]
a worse result than we expected [indirect: licensed by 'worse']
enough money to buy the car [indirect: licensed by 'enough']

statement: In some NPs the head is fused with a dependent, so one word functions as head and as determiner or modifier; words like 'any' and 'several' in such uses are determinatives, not pronouns.
condition: Applies to NPs with no separate head noun where one word is both head and determiner (some, any, several) or head and modifier (the rich, the cheaper of the two).

correct.text: I need some pens but can't find any.
I chose the cheaper of the two.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Traditional grammar calls these pronouns; Cambridge says determinatives.

statement: A genitive NP typically functions as subject-determiner in a larger NP, combining determiner and subject-complement functions; it can fuse with the head ('Mara's was better').
condition: Applies to genitive NPs inside an NP: they mark the NP as definite and function as its subject; in 'the behaviour of the minister' the determiner and complement are realised separately; the genitive may be fused with the head when the head is omitted.

correct.text: the advice of the teacher [determiner 'the' + internal complement]
Your plan failed, but Mara's worked. [fused genitive]

concept: singular count nouns need a determiner
statement: A singular count noun cannot in general head an NP without a determiner.
condition: Applies to NPs whose head is a singular noun in a count sense and whose function is subject or object: such an NP generally requires a determiner. Bare role NPs used as predicative complements are an explicit exception.
violation: A singular count common noun occurs as a subject or object with no determiner, outside the bare-role predicative-complement exception.

exceptions.description: Bare role NPs such as president or deputy leader can occur without a determiner as predicative complements with verbs such as be, become, appoint, and elect; this exception does not license the same bare singular NP as subject or object.

correct.text: I met the president after class.
The members elected Noor deputy leader.

review_notes: Hedged by the source ('in general'). Do not flag cases like bare plurals, non-count nouns or proper nouns: those are outside the rule's scope; unlisted exceptions with count nouns need Ch. 5. Refined with the explicit bare-role-NP exception from Cambridge Ch. 5 §1, p. 328; the owner approved this refinement on 2026-11-05. Bare role NPs are permitted as predicative complements but not as bare singular subject/object NPs.

statement: The adjective is the head of an adjective phrase (AdjP), which is the single higher-level unit needed for adjectives; unlike nouns and verbs, adjectives have no subject or determiner function motivating a second higher-level category. AdjP dependents are modifiers or complements; complements follow the head and are usually PPs or clauses.
condition: Applies to adjective-headed phrases: analyse the adjective and its dependents as an AdjP; there is no further higher-level unit analogous to nominal/NP or VP/clause, since adjectives have no subject or determiner function. Modifiers precede the head; complements follow it and are usually PPs or clauses.

exceptions.description: Only one or two adjectives are transitive and can take an NP complement directly; the source names worth and like. Most adjective-related NPs are instead linked through a preposition.

correct.text: She is ashamed of him. [PP complement]
I'm glad you could come. [clause complement]
the minister responsible for the decision [complement in postpositive AdjP]
The old camera is worth a careful inspection.
correct.note: Worth takes a direct NP complement.

correct.text: The twins are very like each other.
correct.note: Like is one of the rare transitive adjectives identified in the source.
The NP is linked to the adjective through a preposition.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Hedges ('hardly permitted', 'minor exceptions') are preserved; do not turn into constraints without Ch. 6. Cambridge Ch. 6 §1, pp. 526–527, confirms the single AdjP level and explains that adjectives in be + adjective constructions provide the main semantic predicate. It also identifies worth and like as rare transitive adjectives; the ordinary pattern relates an NP to an adjective through a preposition.

statement: The adverb is the head of an adverb phrase (AdvP), the single higher-level unit needed for adverbs; AdvP can be expanded in ways that are broadly a subset of those available to AdjPs, in part because adverbs have no predicative function.
condition: Applies to adverb-headed phrases: analyse the adverb and its dependents as an AdvP; there is no further higher-level unit analogous to nominal/NP or VP/clause. Adverbs allow a narrower range of phrase expansion than adjectives, broadly a subset of AdjP options, and only a very small number license complements.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Cambridge Ch. 6 §1, p. 527, explicitly states that the possible ways of expanding AdvPs are broadly a subset of those for AdjPs and attributes the reduced possibilities at least partly to adverbs having no predicative function. This is a qualified descriptive generalization, not an exceptionless statement.

statement: In a PP the NP in 'to you' or 'of the house' is a complement of the preposition, and modifiers like 'a few minutes' or 'straight' before or after the preposition are modifiers; complements may be objects or predicatives (as a liability) and a PP may have no complement.
condition: Applies to PPs: complement = NP object, predicative (after 'as'), AdvP or clause; modifiers precede the preposition phrase; a complement-less PP is allowed (before, afterwards).

correct.text: They regard him as a liability.
It strikes me as quite reasonable.
They came from behind the barn. [PP complement nested within PP]
The council argued on whether the road should close. [clause complement]
The children waited just inside the fence. [modifier just]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Ch. 7 §1 p. 599 further supports PP, AdvP, clause, and predicative AdjP complements and modifiers within PPs. No NP-only restriction is implied.

statement: The most central prepositions can be stranded, i.e. left with a gap in complement position, when their complement is prenuclear in an interrogative or relative clause; the alternative is to keep the PP together in prenuclear position.
condition: Applies to central prepositions (to, with) in open interrogatives and relative clauses: the PP can be in prenuclear position, or the preposition is stranded with its complement realised by a co-indexed gap.

correct.text: She was talking to a man.
To whom was she talking? [PP prenuclear]
the razor-blade with which I cut it [PP prenuclear]
the razor-blade that I cut it with [stranded]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Only the 'most central' prepositions; which ones are not listed here. Do not use as an error rule. Ch. 7 §1 p. 602 explicitly confines stranding to non-canonical constructions such as interrogatives and relatives and contrasts it with internal complement-head reversal (e.g. notwithstanding).

concept: functions of NPs beyond clause complements
statement: Besides subject, object, and predicative-complement functions in clause structure, NPs can function as PP complements, subject-determiners in NPs, clause adjuncts, modifiers in AdjPs, AdvPs and PPs, supplements, and vocatives.
condition: When classifying an NP in context, consider the larger constituent it combines with: an NP may be a complement within a PP, a subject-determiner inside a larger NP, an adjunct or modifier, a supplement, or a vocative rather than a clause-level subject, object, or predicative complement.

exceptions.description: The source says the adjunct, modifier, supplement, and vocative functions illustrated in [6iii–ix] accept only a restricted range of NPs; one or two NP expressions are specialised for modifying functions and do not occur as clause complements.

contrast.text: The hikers spoke to the guide. [the guide: complement of a preposition]
Mara’s notes were missing. [Mara’s: subject-determiner in an NP]
We waited three hours. [three hours: clause adjunct]
The shelf was two metres high. [two metres: modifier in an AdjP]
They arrived two hours late. [two hours: modifier in an AdvP]
The wreck lay a mile under the sea. [a mile: modifier in a PP]
We met Lina, an experienced guide. [an experienced guide: supplement]
Ava, your taxi is here. [Ava: vocative]
contrast.note: Illustrates a non-clausal NP function; the source restricts the range of NPs available for this and related peripheral functions.

contrast.text: The shelf was a good deal too narrow. [a good deal: NP modifier in an AdjP]
contrast.note: Tests an NP expression specialised for modifier use.

statement: In the aggregate senses here, item of selects clothing rather than clothes, and piece of selects jewellery rather than valuables.
condition: When item or piece packages an individual member in an ordinary of-phrase with the stated aggregate meaning.
violation: The partitive head and the aggregate noun are incompatible in this construction.

exceptions.description: A plural object can occur in a different construction, such as an item from a set, and these nouns may have other senses.

correct.text: One item of clothing was left in the locker.
A piece of jewellery was hidden inside the parcel.

incorrect.text: One item of clothes was left in the locker.
A piece of valuables was hidden inside the parcel.

concept: Plural agreement with cattle and police
statement: In ordinary livestock and law-enforcement senses, cattle and police take plural agreement as subject heads despite lacking an overt plural suffix.
condition: When cattle refers to the animals or police refers to officers collectively, and heads the subject.
violation: The finite verb has the wrong number for the subject head in the specified sense.

exceptions.description: Different heads or constructions can take singular agreement, including herd and police force.

correct.text: The cattle are gathering by the gate.
The police have reopened the bridge.

incorrect.text: The cattle is gathering by the gate.
The police has reopened the bridge.

concept: Rounded group counts and poultry senses

exceptions.description: Poultry meaning meat is singular noncount. People and folk differ in permitting small numerals in their count readings.
